title: home-solar-installation-guide
summary: A guide to planning, installing, and maintaining a home solar panel system. It covers pre-purchase checks (roof suitability such as orientation, shade, and at least 20 square meters of usable area, plus building, electrical, and utility permits), equipment comparisons (monocrystalline, polycrystalline, and thin-film panels in a table of efficiency, price, and lifespan; string inverters vs. microinverters; when batteries are worth it), installation steps (mounting, wiring, and inspection), and maintenance (cleaning methods and troubleshooting power loss or ground faults). Use it for questions on roof requirements, panel types and efficiency, inverter and battery choices, installation or permitting steps, cleaning, and fault response.

children.title: Before You Start
children.summary: Covers the two checks to do before buying solar panels: whether the roof is suitable (south-facing in the northern hemisphere, little shade, good condition, at least 20 square meters of usable area for a typical home) and what permits and approvals are needed (building and electrical permits, plus utility approval for grid connection). Useful for questions about roof requirements, panel lifespan, or permitting steps. No tables or images.
children.text:
Is your roof suitable?
A south-facing roof (in the northern hemisphere) with little shade gives the best output. The roof should be in good condition, because panels last 25 years or more and removing them to repair the roof is costly. Aim for at least 20 square meters of usable area for a typical home.

Permits and codes
Most areas require a building permit and an electrical permit. Your utility may also need to approve a grid connection before you switch the system on. Check local rules before you buy any equipment.

children.title: Choosing Equipment
children.summary: Compares the main components of a solar setup: three panel types (monocrystalline, polycrystalline, thin-film) with a table of typical efficiency, price, and lifespan notes; string inverters versus microinverters; and when a battery is worth its added cost. Useful for questions about panel efficiency ranges, which panel type is cheapest or takes the most roof space, how inverters convert power, and when batteries make sense.
children.text:
Panels
Three panel types are common. Efficiency is the share of sunlight turned into electricity.

| Type | Typical efficiency | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monocrystalline | 20 to 22 percent | Best output per area, highest price |
| Polycrystalline | 15 to 17 percent | Lower price, needs more roof space |
| Thin-film | 10 to 13 percent | Light and flexible, shortest lifespan |

Inverters
The inverter converts the direct current from the panels into alternating current for your home. A single string inverter is cheapest. Microinverters sit under each panel and keep the rest producing when one panel is shaded.

Batteries
A battery stores extra daytime power for use at night or during an outage. It adds cost, and is most useful where the grid is unreliable or where electricity is cheaper at night.

children.title: Installation Steps
children.summary: Covers the three stages of installing a solar panel system: mounting (fixing roof anchors into rafters, sealing holes, attaching rails, leaving about 10 cm of air gap under the panels), wiring (series strings, cable run to the inverter, DC isolator switch, and safety precautions because panels produce voltage in light), and inspection (local inspector approval before grid connection, keeping permits and datasheets). Use it to answer questions about how to mount, wire, or get approval for a installed solar array. No tables or images.
children.text:
Mounting
Fix the roof anchors into the rafters, seal each hole against water, then attach the rails. Leave a gap of about ten centimeters under the panels so air can cool them.

Wiring
Connect the panels in series strings, run the cable to the inverter, and fit a DC isolator switch. Always cover the panels or work in low light, because they produce voltage whenever light falls on them.

Inspection
Have the local inspector approve the work before it is connected to the grid. Keep the permit papers and the equipment datasheets for your records.

children.title: Maintenance and Troubleshooting
children.summary: Covers how to clean solar panels (rain is usually enough; in dusty areas, rinse with water once or twice a year early in the morning, avoiding abrasive pads and pressure washers) and what to do when output suddenly drops (check the inverter display for an error code, suspect a loose connector or shading if one string is affected, and turn the system off and call a qualified electrician for a ground fault). Useful for questions about panel cleaning methods, troubleshooting power loss, and ground fault response. No tables or images.
children.text:
Cleaning
Rain keeps most panels clean enough. In dusty areas, rinse them with water once or twice a year in the early morning. Do not use abrasive pads or a pressure washer.

Common faults
If output falls suddenly, check the inverter display for an error code first. A drop on one string often means a loose connector or a shaded panel. If the inverter shows a ground fault, turn the system off and call a qualified electrician.
